title: Macroeconomic stabilization can coexist with mass informality when growth does not reach productive work, infrastructure, and household earnings
source_unit: World Bank Group, Zimbabwe Growth and Jobs Report, summarized in Zimbabwe Must Leverage Macroeconomic Stability to Accelerate Growth and Create 230,000 New Jobs by 2040, September 4, 2026
geography: Zimbabwe, with national labor-market, infrastructure, macroeconomic, and household-income implications

observations.period: Early 2026 and 2021–2025; macroeconomic stability versus lived economic security

denominator.unit: Zimbabwe national growth and jobs report context

inflation.value: local-currency inflation reached single digits in early 2026, reportedly for the first time since 1997

growth.value: real GDP growth averaged nearly 6% between 2021 and 2025

translation_gap.value: the report says stabilization and growth had not yet generated widespread improvements in productive employment or household incomes

observations.method: World Bank country growth-and-jobs report summarized in an official press release.
observations.uncertainty: The press release does not provide the full distributional time series, causal decomposition, or household panel needed to identify which channels prevented growth from reaching incomes.
observations.subgroup: Workers, informal households, low-income households, young people, firms, and communities affected by macroeconomic and infrastructure conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Macroeconomic stabilization may be a necessary precondition whose benefits arrive with delay; the absence of immediate household gains does not show that stabilization failed.

denominator.unit: percent of Zimbabweans reported to work in the informal sector

informal_work.unit: percent of workers in the informal sector

median_earnings.unit: US dollars per month median informal-sector earnings

sector_shift.value: labor has shifted largely from agriculture into low-productivity retail and informal services rather than formal manufacturing or high-value services

poverty.value: nearly half the population is reported to live below the international poverty line

observations.method: World Bank labor-market and structural-transformation analysis as summarized in the official release.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not specify the reference year, earnings distribution, unpaid work, gender and age breakdowns, or the boundary between informal self-employment and enterprise activity.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers, agricultural workers, retail and service workers, young people entering work, and households dependent on low and variable earnings.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal work can provide flexibility and entry when formal jobs are scarce, but low median earnings and weak protection can leave households exposed to shocks and limit upward mobility.

observations.period: 2026; electricity, transport, irrigation, and productive opportunity

denominator.unit: percent of GDP estimated to be lost annually from electricity shortages

power_cost.unit: percent of GDP annual cost attributed to electricity shortages

infrastructure_bottlenecks.value: the report identifies power generation and grid reliability, transport corridors, and agricultural irrigation as foundational constraints

household_firm_route.value: reliable power and transport are positioned as conditions for firms to invest, workers to access productive jobs, and households to receive higher and more stable earnings

observations.method: World Bank report priorities and estimated macroeconomic cost summarized in the official release.
observations.uncertainty: The 6.1% estimate is not an observed household loss measure; the release does not identify incidence by firm, region, income, gender, or sector, nor establish which infrastructure investment has the highest return.
observations.subgroup: Firms, workers, farmers, households dependent on electricity and transport, and communities affected by unreliable irrigation or public infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Infrastructure investment can expand capacity without improving affordability or reliability if governance, maintenance, financing, and access remain weak.

baseline_growth.unit: percent average growth through 2030 under the current course

accelerated_gdp.value: accelerated reforms could raise real GDP by an additional 10.7% by 2030 and 26.9% by 2040 above baseline

jobs.unit: potential new jobs by 2040 under accelerated reforms

earnings.unit: percent or more increase in real worker earnings by 2040 under the scenario

reform_route.value: the proposed route combines debt and fiscal repair, infrastructure, simpler regulation, land tenure, commercial justice, credit, and private investment

observations.method: World Bank scenario analysis and policy priorities summarized in an official country-report release.
observations.uncertainty: These are modeled scenarios, not forecasts or observed effects; implementation, political economy, external shocks, job quality, distribution, and formalization remain open.
observations.subgroup: Workers, informal enterprises, young people, firms, investors, households, public agencies, and communities affected by reform and infrastructure allocation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate growth and job creation can coexist with unequal gains, displacement, or weak worker protection if formalization and investment occur without bargaining power, social protection, and accountable institutions.

related_sources.claim: World Bank Zimbabwe economic-update materials provide complementary macroeconomic and reform context.
Malawi INSPIRE-O provides a complementary route from shocks through safety nets, jobs, and delivery capacity.

boundary: This record adds a named macro-to-household route from stabilization and growth through informality, low earnings, power and transport bottlenecks, regulation, investment, formal jobs, and worker earnings. It is a country-report summary with modeled scenarios, not a causal evaluation, household panel, or proof that reforms will create evenly distributed, decent work.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank September 4, 2026 press release was reviewed for inflation and growth context, informality and earnings, poverty, structural transformation, electricity-shortage cost, infrastructure priorities, reform scenarios, jobs, earnings, and policy package.
